extracted.intended_audience: graduate (or advanced undergraduate) students in algebraic geometry; readers of Vakil's 'Foundations of Algebraic Geometry' / Math 216
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, basic properties, constructions, and examples of presheaves, sheaves, stalks, morphisms, OX-modules, and sheafification as presented in a course/textbook chapter on sheaf theory in algebraic geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a presheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: A presheaf F assigns to every open set U a set F(U) (the sections over U) and for each inclusion U ⊂ V a restriction map res_{V,U}: F(V) → F(U), satisfying res_{U,U} = id_{F(U)} and functorial composition (if U ⊂ V ⊂ W then res_{W,U} = res_{V,U} ∘ res_{W,V}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements of F(U) are called sections. Several notations (F(U), Γ(U,F), H^0(U,F)) are in use. Exercise 2.2.A: a presheaf is the same as a contravariant functor from the category of open sets to Sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections and restriction maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections over open sets and restriction maps must obey identity and composition axioms: res_{U,U}=id and restriction maps commute on chains of inclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors familiar behavior (e.g., differentiable or continuous functions). The identity/composition requirements are necessary coherence constraints for the presheaf data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stalks and germs (hands-on and colimit descriptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stalk F_p at a point p is the set of germs: equivalence classes of pairs (f,U) with p∈U and f∈F(U), where (f,U) ~ (g,V) if they agree on some neighborhood W ⊂ U∩V of p. Equivalently, F_p = colim_{p∈U} F(U).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germ of f at p is image of f in F_p. The index category is filtered so the two definitions agree. Warning: 'value at a point' in general does not make sense for arbitrary presheaves, hence the need for germs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf axioms (identity and gluability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A presheaf F is a sheaf if for every open cover {U_i} of U: (Identity) if f1,f2∈F(U) and res_{U,U_i} f1 = res_{U,U_i} f2 for all i then f1=f2; (Gluability) if given compatible fi∈F(U_i) with res_{U_i, U_i∩U_j} fi = res_{U_j, U_i∩U_j} fj for all i,j, then there exists f∈F(U) with res_{U,U_i} f = fi for all i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity = 'at most one way to glue'; gluability = 'at least one way to glue'. A presheaf satisfying identity is called separated. Note about empty set: often F(∅) is required to be the final object; this follows from the axioms in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard examples: sheaves of differentiable, continuous, smooth, or holomorphic functions; sheaf of continuous maps to a fixed topological space Y; sheaf of sections of a map µ: Y→X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 2.2.D, 2.2.F, 2.2.G ask to verify these. These examples motivate terminology like 'section of a sheaf' and show how geometric data give sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of a sheaf to an open subset
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a sheaf on X and U⊂X is open, the restriction F|_U defined by F|_U(V)=F(V) for V⊂U is a sheaf on U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a basic functorial construction; later sections show how to restrict to arbitrary subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skyscraper sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: Given p∈X and a set S, define i_{p,*}S(U)=S if p∈U and = {e} (a one-element set) if p∉U. This forms a sheaf (called a skyscraper sheaf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous definitions exist for sheaves of groups or modules. Caution: the informal picture 'only nontrivial stalk at p' can be misleading—there are examples where other stalks are nontrivial (see Exercise 13.2.A(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant presheaf vs constant sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: The constant presheaf Spre has Spre(U)=S for all U (with identity restrictions) and is generally not a sheaf. The constant sheaf associated to S consists of locally constant maps to S (equivalently continuous maps to S with discrete topology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 2.2.E: show the locally-constant-map description is a sheaf. The failure of Spre to be a sheaf can be seen on simple spaces (e.g., a two-point discrete space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf of sections of a map (motivation for 'sections')
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a continuous map µ: Y→X, the assignment to U⊂X of continuous maps s:U→Y with µ∘s = id|_U forms a sheaf (the sheaf of sections of µ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction includes the sheaf of sections of vector bundles; if Y is a topological group, continuous maps to Y form a sheaf of groups (Exercise 2.2.G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Espace étalé (space of sections) construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a presheaf F, form the disjoint union of all stalks and topologize it so that subsets coming from sections { (x, s_x) : x∈U } are open; this yields a topological space π: F → X (the espace étalé) with local homeomorphism properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each section s∈F(U) determines an open subset of the espace étalé. This viewpoint helps interpret pullback, pushforward, and sheafification (see Remark 2.4.8 and Exercise 2.2.G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushforward / direct image sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: For π: X→Y continuous and F a presheaf on X, define π_*F(V)=F(π^{-1}(V)). Then π_*F is a presheaf on Y and is a sheaf if F is a sheaf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 2.2.H: verify pushforward preserves the sheaf property. Pushforward is a functor from sheaves on X to sheaves on Y (Exercise 2.3.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ringed space and OX-module structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A ringed space (X, OX) has a structure sheaf OX of rings; an OX-module F is a sheaf of abelian groups such that for each U, F(U) is an OX(U)-module and the module action commutes with restriction maps (commutative compatibility diagram (2.2.13.1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections of the structure sheaf are called 'functions'. Vector bundle sections provide the motivating example: sections can be multiplied by functions and restriction commutes with multiplication (Exercise 2.2.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms of (pre)sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism φ: F→G is a collection of maps φ(U):F(U)→G(U) compatible with restriction maps (commuting squares). For presheaves interpreted as contravariant functors, morphisms are natural transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morphisms induce maps on stalks φ_p: F_p → G_p (Exercise 2.3.A). The category of sheaves on X is a full subcategory of presheaves. Example: forgetful map from differentiable to continuous functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms determined by stalks
rubrics_metrics.description: For morphisms F→G where G is a sheaf, if two morphisms induce the same maps on all stalks then they are equal; moreover a morphism of sheaves is an isomorphism iff it induces isomorphisms on all stalks (Exercises 2.4.D and 2.4.E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses the injectivity of the map F(U)→∏_{p∈U} F_p for sheaves (sections determined by germs) and gluability to get surjectivity when checking isomorphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf Hom (internal Hom) and its behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Hom(F,G)(U) := Mor(F|_U, G|_U). This assignment is a sheaf (called sheaf Hom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In additive contexts use Hom_{AbX} or Hom_{Mod_OX}. Warning: sheaf Hom does not commute with taking stalks — Hom(F,G)_p is not in general isomorphic to Hom(F_p, G_p).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additive/abelian category structure for (pre)sheaves of abelian groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Presheaves (and sheaves) of abelian groups form additive categories. Kernels may be formed objectwise; presheaf kernels are sheaves, so kernel in sheaves is the presheaf kernel. Cokernels in sheaves require sheafification of the presheaf cokernel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define ker^{pre} φ(U)=ker(φ(U)). The presheaf cokernel must be sheafified to get the cokernel in sheaves. This explains why sheafification is needed for cokernels and similar colimit constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties determined at the level of stalks (sections, supports, mono/epi)
rubrics_metrics.description: For sheaves: (a) sections are determined by their germs (F(U)→∏_{p∈U} F_p is injective); (b) the image of this map consists of 'compatible germs' and any compatible choice of germs arises from a section (gluability); (c) support Supp(s):={p | s_p≠0} is closed; (d) φ is monomorphism iff φ_p injective for all p; (e) φ is epimorphism iff φ_p surjective for all p (for sheaves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 2.4.A–2.4.O develop these facts; counterexamples show these fail for general presheaves (Exercise 2.4.F). Use skyscraper sheaves and local arguments when proving epimorphism equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheafification (definition, construction, and universal property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a presheaf F, a sheafification sh: F → F^{sh} is a morphism to a sheaf F^{sh} with the universal property that any morphism from F to a sheaf G factors uniquely through F^{sh}. A concrete construction: F^{sh}(U) = set of compatible germs (families (f_x)_x with local representatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sheafification is unique up to unique isomorphism (Exercise 2.4.G), is functorial (Exercise 2.4.H), is left adjoint to the forgetful functor, and induces isomorphisms on stalks (Exercise 2.4.M). The 'espace étalé' viewpoint gives an alternate construction (Remark 2.4.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernels and cokernels at the level of stalks
rubrics_metrics.description: For a morphism φ: F→G of sheaves of abelian groups, (ker φ)_x ≅ ker(F_x → G_x) and the stalk of the cokernel equals the cokernel of the stalk maps after sheafifying the presheaf cokernel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition/Exercise 2.5.A–2.5.B: the sheaf cokernel is obtained by sheafifying the presheaf cokernel; stalkwise exactness statements follow accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exponential exact sequence example (illustrating local vs global surjectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: On X=ℂ (classical topology), 0 → ℤ → O_X → O_X^* → 1 where the map ℤ→O_X is multiplication by 2πi and exp: O_X → O_X^* is the exponential. Locally invertible holomorphic functions have logarithms, but not necessarily globally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This example (Exercise 2.4.10 and 2.4.P) illustrates that a morphism can be surjective on stalks yet fail to be surjective on global sections, and clarifies the meaning of surjectivity for sheaves.
